questions.prompt: Augustine's most famous line, from the opening of the Confessions, reads 'Cor nostrum inquietum est, donec requiescat in te.' What does it say?
choices: Our heart is restless until it rests in you
Our heart is silent until it speaks of you
Our mind is troubled until it understands you
Our soul is weak until it serves you
questions.correctAnswer: Our heart is restless until it rests in you
questions.explanation: 'Inquietum' -- literally 'un-quieted' -- names the restlessness, and 'requiescat' -- 'may it rest' -- names the only cure Augustine will accept for it. The whole Confessions is essentially one long argument for this single opening sentence.
questions.hint: 'Requiescat' is the same root behind the funeral prayer 'requiescat in pace' -- rest in peace.

questions.prompt: True or False: Tertullian's phrase 'Anima naturaliter Christiana' -- 'the soul is naturally Christian' -- claims every person is born already believing explicit Christian doctrine.
questions.explanation: False. Tertullian's point is narrower and more interesting: even pagan speech unconsciously invokes the true God in moments of surprise or fear, suggesting the soul has a natural orientation toward him -- not that doctrine is innate, but that the soul's deepest instincts already point where explicit faith later leads.
questions.hint: Ask whether 'naturally oriented toward' and 'already explicitly believing' are the same claim.

questions.prompt: St. Vincent of Lérins gave the classic test for authentic tradition in Latin as 'quod ubique, quod semper, quod ab ____' -- what has been believed everywhere, always, and by all.
questions.explanation: 'Omnibus' is dative/ablative plural of 'omnis,' all -- the same root that gives English 'omnibus' (a vehicle for everyone) and 'omniscient.' The threefold test names where, when, and by whom, in that order.
questions.hint: This word gives English a word for a vehicle that carries everyone.

questions.prompt: Dei Verbum 25 quotes St. Jerome's maxim, in Latin 'Ignoratio Scripturarum ignoratio Christi est.' What does it claim?
choices: Ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ
Knowledge of Scripture replaces the need to know Christ personally
The Scriptures are too difficult for ordinary believers to understand
Christ is known only apart from the Scriptures
questions.correctAnswer: Ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ
questions.explanation: Vatican II found this fourth-century line important enough to quote directly, urging all the faithful toward frequent reading of Scripture on the strength of Jerome's own maxim -- a patristic voice given fresh authority eight centuries later.
questions.hint: The same word, 'ignoratio,' appears twice, once about Scripture and once about Christ.

questions.prompt: True or False: The maxim 'Extra Ecclesiam nulla salus' (outside the Church there is no salvation), already met earlier in this topic, is traditionally attributed to St. Cyprian of Carthage.
questions.explanation: True. Cyprian's third-century formulation is the origin of the phrase; its later, careful interpretation -- distinguishing formal from invincible ignorance -- is a separate development this database covers elsewhere, but the phrase itself is genuinely patristic in origin, not a later invention.
questions.hint: This is the same Latin phrase from Level 4 -- the new information here is who first said it.

questions.prompt: Why does this database treat 'Roma locuta, causa finita est' ('Rome has spoken, the matter is settled') with caution when attributing it to Augustine?
choices: It is a later summary of Augustine's actual argument, not a sentence he wrote verbatim in this exact form
Because Augustine never discussed Rome's authority at all
Because the phrase is entirely modern in origin, with no patristic root
Because the phrase was formally condemned by a later council
questions.correctAnswer: It is a later summary of Augustine's actual argument, not a sentence he wrote verbatim in this exact form
questions.explanation: Augustine did argue, in the Pelagian controversy, that Rome's judgment settled the matter -- but the pithy Latin tag itself is a later distillation of that argument, not a verified direct quotation. This level's whole point is telling the two apart: real influence does not always come with an exact matching sentence.
questions.hint: Ask whether a phrase capturing someone's real argument is the same as a verified direct quotation.

questions.prompt: Jerome's maxim on Scripture and Christ was important enough for the Second Vatican Council to quote directly, in the document Dei ____.
questions.explanation: 'Dei Verbum' -- 'the Word of God' -- is Vatican II's constitution on divine revelation, and its own title uses the same word, 'Verbum,' that opens John's Gospel in Latin.
questions.hint: 'Verbum' is Latin for 'Word' -- the same word John's Gospel uses for Christ himself.

questions.prompt: True or False: Reading a Church Father's Latin directly, rather than only a translation, can surface a precise word choice -- like Augustine's 'inquietum' -- that an English rendering may soften or lose.
questions.explanation: True, and this is the whole reason a level on Patristic Latin belongs in this topic. 'Restless' is a fair translation of 'inquietum,' but the Latin's own shape -- 'un-quieted,' built from the same root as 'requiescat' two words later -- creates an echo within the sentence that translation alone does not preserve.
questions.hint: Compare 'inquietum' and 'requiescat' -- do they share a root in the Latin the way 'restless' and 'rest' barely do in English?

questions.prompt: What does reading Vincent of Lérins's threefold test in its original Latin word order -- ubique, semper, ab omnibus -- preserve that a looser paraphrase might lose?
choices: The deliberate sequence: place, then time, then people, building the case cumulatively in that specific order
Nothing; word order carries no meaning in Latin
That the three tests must be applied in reverse order
That only the third test, 'ab omnibus,' actually matters
questions.correctAnswer: The deliberate sequence: place, then time, then people, building the case cumulatively in that specific order
questions.explanation: Vincent builds his case in a specific order -- everywhere, then always, then by everyone -- moving from geography to history to universal human witness. A paraphrase that reorders the three loses the sense of a case being built, term by term.
questions.hint: Ask whether the three tests are simply listed, or built up in a deliberate sequence.

Actually repeat it confidently as a real, genuine quotation, since it sounds authentically patristic
Actually assume every real, Latin tag found online is automatically, genuinely fabricated, with no possible, real exception
The real, honest, practical rule is actually to ignore the question of a real source entirely

questions.explanation: This is exactly the same real, honest method the previous level already modeled with 'Roma locuta, causa finita est' -- treating an unsourced, real tag as genuinely unverified until a real, specific, citable source can actually be found.

questions.prompt: 'Dominus vobiscum' -- 'The Lord be with you' -- fuses 'cum' with the pronoun 'vobis' as 'vobiscum,' placing 'cum' after the pronoun rather than before it. What is this an example of?
choices: A regular feature of Latin grammar: the personal pronouns place 'cum' after themselves (mecum, tecum, secum, nobiscum, vobiscum), reversing the usual preposition-then-noun order
A unique, one-off exception found only in this specific liturgical phrase
An error introduced by a medieval copyist
A feature found only in ecclesiastical, not classical, Latin
questions.correctAnswer: A regular feature of Latin grammar: the personal pronouns place 'cum' after themselves (mecum, tecum, secum, nobiscum, vobiscum), reversing the usual preposition-then-noun order
questions.explanation: This is ordinary classical Latin grammar, not a liturgical peculiarity -- 'cum' regularly follows rather than precedes the personal pronouns as one fused word, in exactly the pattern 'vobiscum' shows.
questions.hint: Compare 'vobiscum' to 'mecum' and 'tecum' -- the same pattern, different pronoun each time.

questions.prompt: True or False: In the Agnus Dei, 'qui tollis peccata mundi,' the verb 'tollis' is second person singular -- addressing Christ directly as 'thou who takest away' rather than describing him in the third person.
questions.explanation: True, and the grammar itself carries theology: English translations often render this 'who takes away,' which sounds like a description, where the Latin's second-person 'tollis' makes the whole line a direct address to Christ -- the same pattern already met in 'Domine, non sum dignus' earlier in this topic.
questions.hint: Compare this to the second-person address already met in 'Domine, non sum dignus.'

questions.prompt: Many Collects in the Roman Missal close with a purpose clause introduced by 'ut' followed by a subjunctive verb (for example, '...ut mereamur' -- 'that we may deserve/attain'). What does 'ut + subjunctive' signal here?
choices: Purpose -- the goal or result the prayer is asking God to bring about
A simple statement of fact with no request involved
A direct command addressed to the congregation
A quotation from an earlier speaker
questions.correctAnswer: Purpose -- the goal or result the prayer is asking God to bring about
questions.explanation: 'Ut' triggering the subjunctive is a standard Latin purpose construction: 'so that' something may result. Recognizing this pattern lets a reader spot the actual request buried at the end of a long Collect, rather than losing it in the sentence's length.
questions.hint: 'Ut' with the subjunctive typically answers the question 'to what end?'

questions.prompt: In 'Sursum corda,' 'corda' is the direct object of an implied command verb, 'levate' -- lift. 'Corda' is accusative plural of 'cor, cordis,' meaning ____.
questions.explanation: 'Cor, cordis' is heart -- the root behind 'cordial' and 'courage.' 'Sursum corda' compresses an entire imperative sentence ('Lift up your hearts') into two words, with the verb itself left understood.
questions.hint: The root gives English 'cordial' and 'courage' -- both, in different ways, about the heart.

questions.prompt: True or False: 'Credo in unum Deum,' the Creed's opening, uses 'credo' with 'in' plus the accusative, a construction distinct from ordinary Latin verbs of believing, which normally take the dative alone.
questions.explanation: True, and it is a real, noticed feature of Christian Latin: classical Latin more often expresses trust in a person with the simple dative, while 'credere in' with the accusative is a construction that develops and spreads specifically in Christian usage -- the grammar itself marking out something distinctively Christian about the act of faith.
questions.hint: Ask whether this exact grammatical construction was already standard in classical, pre-Christian Latin.

questions.prompt: 'Corpus Christi' and 'Corpus Domini' are both genitive constructions -- 'Body of Christ,' 'Body of the Lord.' What does the genitive case do grammatically in both phrases?
choices: Shows possession or close relation -- whose body it is
Marks the subject performing an action
Marks the direct object receiving an action
Indicates the location where something happens
questions.correctAnswer: Shows possession or close relation -- whose body it is
questions.explanation: The genitive is Latin's possessive case, here linking 'body' to whose body is meant. Recognizing the genitive by its typical endings (-i, -is, and others depending on declension) is one of the most useful single skills for reading any Latin liturgical phrase.
questions.hint: Ask what relationship 'of' typically expresses in English -- that is the genitive's usual job.

questions.prompt: 'Et cum spiritu tuo' -- 'and with your spirit' -- uses 'tuo,' the ablative singular form matching 'spiritu' in gender, number, and case: this agreement is called ____.
questions.explanation: Concord (or agreement) is the rule that an adjective or possessive must match the noun it modifies in gender, number and case -- which is why 'tuo' takes this particular ending to match the masculine ablative singular noun 'spiritu,' rather than a different ending that would match some other noun.
questions.hint: This grammatical term names the requirement that a modifying word 'agree' with the noun it describes.

questions.prompt: True or False: 'Ite, missa est' uses 'missa' as a passive participle related to the verb 'mittere,' to send -- the same root that gives the Mass its own name.
questions.explanation: True, and this closes a loop from Level 1 of this topic: 'missa,' 'sent,' is a form of the same verb that gives English 'mission' and 'missionary' -- the dismissal literally sends the assembly out, which is exactly why the Mass takes its name from this one word.
questions.hint: This is the same root discussed in Level 1, where the Mass's own name was first explained.

questions.prompt: Composing a short original sentence, 'Gratias tibi ago' ('I give thanks to you'), what case is 'tibi'?
choices: Dative -- the indirect object, to or for whom the thanks are given
Genitive -- showing possession
Ablative -- showing means or manner
Vocative -- direct address
questions.correctAnswer: Dative -- the indirect object, to or for whom the thanks are given
questions.explanation: 'Ago' (I do/give) takes 'gratias' as its direct object (accusative) and 'tibi' as its indirect object (dative) -- to whom the thanks are directed. Recognizing this pattern is what lets a reader compose, not merely recognize, a simple original Latin sentence.
questions.hint: Ask who is receiving the thanks, as distinct from what is being given.

questions.explanation: None of these four features is unique to liturgical Latin -- all are ordinary classical grammar. Recognizing them is what turns memorized phrases into a language that can actually be read, rather than a set of vocabulary flashcards.
questions.hint: Ask, for each row, what grammatical job the highlighted word or ending is doing.
